title: Persian Solar Hijri Calendar
intro: The Solar Hijri calendar is a solar calendar used for civil dates in Iran and related traditions. Its new year, Nowruz, begins close to the northern spring equinox. Unlike a lunar calendar, its months remain linked to the seasons.
summary: Twelve months. The first six contain 31 days, the next five contain 30, and the final month usually has 29 (or 30 in a leap year).
origin: The modern civil Solar Hijri system took shape in the twentieth century. This implementation follows the project’s documented ICU-compatible leap corrections, not every older Iranian date convention.
structure: A long summer half and a shorter winter half make the year easy to remember. Leap years add a day to the final month, Esfand.
diagram_caption: SIX LONG MONTHS  /  FIVE MEDIUM  /  ONE VARIABLE
pattern_note: Months are not tied to sightings of the Moon. The calendar's leap-year calculation keeps the new year near the seasonal spring boundary.
history: Nowruz has a long cultural history. Modern Solar Hijri civil month lengths and computation were standardised far later. The official calendars of different countries and centuries should not be treated as automatically identical.
example: Nowruz is the first day of Farvardin, usually falling around 20 or 21 March in Gregorian notation. The exact match depends on the particular year and calendar rule.
limits: The implemented arithmetic is not a reconstruction of historical Iranian month lengths before 1304 AP (1925 CE), nor a blanket guarantee of every equinox-based civil decision.
